title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 24: Mercado v. Tan: Is a Judicial Declaration of Nullity of a Prior Marriage Needed to Abate Bigamy?
keywords: Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code
primary_topics: Chapter 24 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of his ponencia in Mercado v. Tan, holding that a judicial declaration of nullity of a previous marriage is necessary before another may be contracted, and that one who remarries without it is guilty of bigamy.
His reconstruction of the conflicting jurisprudence on the question, from People v. Mendoza and People v. Aragon through Vda. de Consuegra, Tolentino v. Paras, Wiegel, Yap and Domingo v. CA.

The statutory turn on which the case rests: the old rulings were moored on Section 29 of Act No. 3613, while Article 40 of the Family Code, a new provision, expressly requires a final judgment declaring the prior marriage void before remarriage.

The application to the accused, who sought annulment of his first marriage only after a bigamy complaint had been filed, and CJP's warning that the contrary view 'effectively encourages delay in the prosecution of bigamy cases.'
sub_topics: He states the problem: bigamy under Article 349 punishes contracting a second marriage before the former is legally dissolved, and asks whether the charge still prospers when the first marriage is void from the beginning.
The holding: a judicial declaration of nullity is necessary, and 'one who enters into a subsequent marriage without first obtaining such judicial declaration is guilty of bigamy.'

The simple facts: Vincent Paul G. Mercado married Thelma Oliva on April 10, 1976 and Consuelo Tan on June 27, 1991; Tan filed a bigamy complaint on October 5, 1992, and only on November 13, 1992 did Mercado sue to annul the first marriage for psychological incapacity, obtaining a decree on May 6, 1993.
Mercado's argument that a void marriage 'is deemed never to have taken place at all,' so there was no first marriage to speak of.

The jurisprudential survey: Mendoza and Aragon acquitted on the theory that no declaration was needed; Vda. de Consuegra v. GSIS and Wiegel v. Sempio-Diy stressed the need for one; Tolentino v. Paras and Yap v. CA went the other way; and Domingo v. CA declared that the Family Code had settled the conflict.
His distinction that Domingo was a civil case, so as author of the Decision he had to justify why a judicial declaration is also essential in a criminal prosecution for bigamy.

The statutory excavation: Section 29 of Act No. 3613 made a subsequent marriage illegal and void from its performance with no decree needed, a provision carried substantially into Article 83 of the 1950 Civil Code and Article 41 of the Family Code -- but Article 40 is new and expressly demands a final judgment.
The conclusion that the statutory mooring of Mendoza and Aragon 'has been cast aside by Article 40 of the Family Code,' so that absent the declaration one may be charged with and convicted of bigamy.

Supporting authority: Terre v. Terre, where the Court called a second marriage contracted without such a declaration 'bigamous and criminal in character,' a Civil Law authority on the Civil Code Revision Committee, and Justice Reyes, a Criminal Law authority who changed his published view in 1993.

The application: Mercado contracted the second marriage with no declaration in hand and filed his nullity petition only after the letter-complaint, so the crime had already been consummated and the later decree was immaterial.
The policy warning that allowing the belated petition would let an accused invoke its pendency as a prejudicial question, which the Court 'cannot allow.'

Justice Vitug's separate view that the requirement should refer only to cases where a marriage at least ostensibly took place -- not, for instance, a purported marriage between persons of the same sex or without consent -- and that the Family Code did not overturn the rule in criminal law, since Article 349 contemplated an existing rather than a void prior marriage.
CJP's answer that the observation deserves reflection but does not apply here, because the Mercado first marriage had actually been celebrated and was attacked only under Article 36.

The postscript on Bobis v. Bobis, penned by Justice Consuelo Ynares-Santiago and promulgated almost the same day, holding that a later civil action for nullity is not a prejudicial question and that 'respondent cannot be permitted to use his own malfeasance to defeat the criminal action against him.'

stances.rhetorical_move: resolving conflicting precedents by locating the statutory basis each rested on and showing that Article 40 of the Family Code displaced it

notable_anecdotes: CJP explains that because Domingo v. CA was merely a civil case, he had to dig up the statutory basis of the earlier rulings himself to justify extending the requirement to a criminal prosecution.
He notes that Mercado instituted the action to annul his first marriage only after the complainant had filed a letter-complaint charging him with bigamy.
He records that Justice Reyes, the Criminal Law authority whose earlier work the petitioner had cited, had himself changed his view in 1993 because of Article 40.

He concedes that Justice Vitug's observation deserves reflection, granting that where a first 'marriage' was a total sham like one in a movie no declaration would be needed -- but showing why Mercado was not such a case.

He adds as a postscript that his Decision was strengthened by Bobis v. Bobis, a unanimous First Division case promulgated almost on the same day, which held the nullity suit not to be a prejudicial question.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 24 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' presents Mercado v. Tan, in which CJP's ponencia held that a judicial declaration of nullity of a previous marriage is necessary before another may be contracted, and that one who remarries without it commits bigamy. Vincent Paul G. Mercado married Thelma Oliva in 1976 and Consuelo Tan in 1991; Tan filed a bigamy complaint in October 1992, and only afterwards did Mercado sue to annul the first marriage for psychological incapacity, obtaining a decree in 1993. He argued before the Court that a void marriage is deemed never to have taken place, so there was no first marriage to speak of. CJP answered by first tracing what the Court itself had called conflicting jurisprudence: People v. Mendoza and People v. Aragon had acquitted on the theory that no declaration was needed, Vda. de Consuegra v. GSIS and Wiegel v. Sempio-Diy had stressed that one was, Tolentino v. Paras and Yap v. CA had gone the other way, and Domingo v. CA had declared that the Family Code settled the matter. Because Domingo was a civil case, he had to justify the requirement in a criminal prosecution, which he did by showing that Mendoza and Aragon rested on Section 29 of Act No. 3613, carried into Article 83 of the Civil Code and Article 41 of the Family Code, whereas Article 40 was a new provision expressly requiring a final judgment. That statutory mooring having been cast aside, remarriage without a decree exposes the party to conviction. Mercado's later decree was immaterial, since the crime was already consummated, and his position would encourage delay by letting accused persons invoke pending nullity suits as prejudicial questions. Justice Vitug urged a narrower reading limited to marriages that at least ostensibly occurred; CJP found the observation worth reflection but inapplicable. A postscript cites Bobis v. Bobis, decided almost the same day, holding such a civil action not a prejudicial question.
